summary: Luca Benati's 2015 Journal of Monetary Economics paper uses structural VARs and cointegration methods to test whether the long-run Phillips curve (LRPC) is non-vertical for the post-WWII U.S., U.K., Euro area, Canada, and Australia. Across strong-form, medium-form, and weak-form LRPC specifications, neither approach yields clear evidence of a non-vertical inflation-unemployment trade-off, though uncertainty around the estimates is substantial. The paper extends King and Watson (1994) using six-variable VARs and newer identification methods, and argues Svensson's (2015) inflation-targeting estimates are uninformative about the LRPC slope because inflation has lost its unit root under inflation targeting.
one_line: Benati's 2015 structural VAR study finds no clear evidence of a non-vertical long-run Phillips curve across five advanced economies, though estimates are highly uncertain.
key_facts: The paper was published in the Journal of Monetary Economics, Volume 76, November 2015, pages 15-28, by Luca Benati.
The study examines the long-run trade-off between inflation and the unemployment rate in the post-WWII U.S., U.K., Euro area, Canada, and Australia.
The abstract states that neither cointegration methods nor non-cointegrated structural VARs produce clear evidence of a non-vertical trade-off.
The paper states that the extent of uncertainty surrounding the estimates is substantial, so a researcher with alternative priors likely would not see her views falsified.
The long-run Phillips curve is defined as describing the alternative combinations of inflation and the unemployment rate that an economy can achieve in equilibrium.
King and Watson (1994) produced evidence of a negative and statistically significant long-run trade-off conditional on aggregate demand-side shocks, using a bivariate VAR.
Evans (1994) showed that trivariate VARs based on King and Watson's identification strategy sometimes pointed towards a vertical long-run Phillips curve.
The paper uses six-variable VARs with information about the stance of monetary policy and the state of the business cycle.
The 'strong-form LRPC' tests whether inflation and unemployment are possibly cointegrated; evidence for it was overall weak.
The 'medium-form LRPC' allows permanent inflation shocks, not further disentangled, to have a permanent impact on the unemployment rate; for neither country was it possible to reject a vertical LRPC.

The 'weak-form LRPC' disentangles permanent inflation shocks into demand- and supply-side shocks using sign restrictions on impacts at t=0; for none of the four identified shocks is there evidence of a non-vertical LRPC.
The monetary policy shock is described as the single most important of the identified shocks for the slope of the LRPC.
Benati (2008) documented that under inflation targeting, evidence of a unit root in inflation has entirely vanished, with inflation in most cases statistically indistinguishable from white noise.
The conclusions state the evidence provides essentially no support to a non-vertical long-run Phillips trade-off that a policymaker could exploit to permanently reduce unemployment.
